title: the seasons
hook: water warmed by the sun all day and cooled by the moon all night: Charaka's autumn has a name for it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons, and Charaka's rains: a low inner fire, light food, dry feet, and the monks who stay put. Did you keep the pleasure and halve the portion? Day one thousand three hundred six.

Swan water. All day the autumn sun warms it. All night the moon shines on it and it cools. Charaka's chapter on the seasons calls water like that hamsodaka, and says, paraphrased, that such water, made clean by time and the stars, is like nectar. Plain water, left out in the open, as a small calendar of the sky. On our last day with the seasons, the year comes round to autumn.
screen: `WARMED BY THE SUN, COOLED BY THE MOON.` → `HAMSODAKA, SWAN WATER.` → `THE YEAR COMES ROUND TO AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: Charaka calls autumn sharad. And his reading, paraphrased, starts with a jolt. Through the rains the body grew used to cool and damp. Then the clouds clear, the sun comes out hard, and the body is suddenly heated. Pitta, the hot, sharp quality, which built up quietly in the rains, flares. So the advice is cooling. Sweet, bitter and astringent foods. Light meals. Ghee prepared with bitter herbs. Avoid too much sun, curds, heavy food, daytime sleep. And then the gentle part: the swan water to drink, and, in the early part of the night, moonlight. Three last things before the year closes. First, autumn shows that a season isn't just its weather. It's the weather after the last one. The same sun means something different after months of rain. Second, the moon. Hindu practice gives autumn a full moon all its own, Sharad Purnima, and in some homes a pot of rice and milk is left out under it overnight, then eaten in the morning. Cooling food, cooled by the moon, in the very season Charaka asks for both. Third, now the whole year can be seen at once. In Charaka's chapter, there are six seasons: two winters, then spring, summer, the rains and autumn. And the same move runs through every one: notice what the season brings, and answer it with its opposite. The fire held in by cold, fed. The thaw, lightened. The heat, cooled with water. The rains, met with care. And autumn's sudden sun, cooled with bitter things and moonlight.
screen: `SHARAD: SUDDEN SUN AFTER RAIN` · `COOL WHAT THE RAINS STORED UP` · `RICE AND MILK UNDER THE MOON` · `SIX SEASONS, ONE MOVE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk once around the year. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a cold morning you remember. Then a spring day. Then real heat. Then rain. Then a clear autumn evening. Stay a breath or two with each, and notice what your body wanted in it: warmth, lightness, water, shelter, cool. Then come back to today, this season, this air, and simply sit in it. If you pray, you can give thanks for the turning year. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. Ritucharya, the conduct of the seasons: six seasons in Charaka's year, and in every one, notice what it brings and answer it with its opposite. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Tonight, step outside for a minute after dark and look for the moon; if it's hidden, just let the night air cool your face. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda cool the body in autumn with bitter and sweet foods and ghee, as the classical texts advise, and on Sharad Purnima some Hindu families leave rice cooked in milk under the full moon overnight.

fork.reveal: Charaka cools autumn: sweet, bitter and astringent food, ghee prepared with bitter herbs, swan water, and moonlight early in the night.

sources.ref: Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 6 (six seasons; sharad: pitta accumulated in the rains aggravated by sudden sun; sweet, bitter, astringent, light food; ghee with bitter herbs; avoid curds, day sleep, heavy food, too much sun; hamsodaka; moonlight early in the night)

notes: Last of the seasons days (1300–1306). Next part is food as practice (1307–1313).
Charaka Sutrasthana 6: confirm that the chapter names six seasons (shishira, vasanta, grishma, varsha, sharad, hemanta) and the sharad regimen as paraphrased.

Hamsodaka: confirm the description (warmed by the sun by day, cooled by the moon by night, purified by the rising of the star Agastya, likened to nectar). 'Made clean by time and the stars' paraphrases the Agastya detail; 'swan water' glosses hamsa + udaka.
Ritucharya used in the word segment as the name of the seasonal regimen; confirm it was introduced on 1300–1301, or keep as a first mention.
Sharad Purnima rice-and-milk (kheer) under the moon: confirm 'in some homes'.
Editor: hook now opens on the name 'swan water' instead of a pot left outside, so it doesn't repeat 1304's clay-pot hook; varied the 'turn it a few ways' transition.
